Recursive functions are obtained in a
	
	roundabout way in our
	interpreter: First bind the name that will refer to the recursive
	function and assign to it the special value

; then define the
	recursive function in the scope of that name; and finally assign the
	defined function to the name. By the time the recursive function gets
	applied, any occurrences of the name in the body properly refer to
	the recursive function. Amazingly, it is possible to specify recursive
	functions without using assignment or function definitions. The following program computes
	10 factorial by applying a recursive
	
	factorial function:
(lambda n: ((lambda fact: (fact(fact, n))) (lambda ft, k: (1 if k == 1 else k * ft(ft, k - 1)))))(10)

solution.body:
# solution provided by GitHub user LucasGdosR

# The Fibonacci function receives n as an argument
# It applies the fib function recursively, passing n as an argument,
# as well as the initial arguments (k = 1, fib1 = 1, fib2 = 1)
(lambda n: (lambda fib: fib(fib, n, 2, 1, 1))
      # The fib function is then defined as ft,
      # with parameters n, k, fib1, and fib2
      # Establish the base cases: n == 1 or n == 2
      (lambda ft, n, k, fib1, fib2:
                  1 if n == 1 else
                  1 if n == 2 else
                  # Iterate until k equals n. Notice k starts at 2, and gets incremented every iteration
                  # When k reaches n, return the accumulated fib2
                  fib2 if k == n else
                  # Otherwise, accumulate the sum as the new fib2
                  ft(ft, n, k + 1, fib2, fib1 + fib2)))

The design of our evaluator of
	section

imposes a
	runtime burden on the application of functions: It needs to scan
	the body of the function for local names, extend the
	environment of the function with a frame that binds the parameters and
	those names, and evaluate the
	body in this extended environment. Alternatively, the application
	of a function could extend the environment of the function with a frame that
	binds only the parameters.
	The evaluation of each assignment and each function definition in the
	body would then add a new binding to that frame, unless the frame
	already binds the name.
	To implement this design, we first simplify

can no
	longer assume that the environment already has a binding for
	the name, and it no longer searches the enclosing frames for a binding
	to change.
	Instead, an assignment always concerns the first frame of the
	environment, which is the frame of the current function application.
	If that frame binds the name, the binding gets the new value.
	Otherwise, the function

adds a binding of the name to the new value to the first frame.
	The same function works at the top level of a program, where the
	first frame is the global frame, and we no longer need to
	test for the global environment.

remains
	unchanged: it still searches the enclosing frames.
	As a consequence, an assignment in a function body creates a new
	local binding even if an enclosing frame already binds the name.

With sequential definition processing, the scope of a local name is
	no longer the entire body of the function, but rather just the portion
	of the evaluation starting at the point where
	the name is declared: Before that point, the name
	refers to a binding in an enclosing frame, if there is one.
	Although we no longer have simultaneous scope, sequential
	definition processing
	will evaluate calls to the function

at the beginning of this section
	correctly, but for an
	"

" reason: Since the definitions
	of the internal functions come first, no calls to these functions
	will be evaluated until all of them have been defined. Hence,
will have been defined by the time

is applied.  In fact, 
	sequential definition processing 
	will give the same result as our scanning-out-names evaluator in
	section

for any function
	in which the 
	
	the declarations of the local names come first
	in the body, and evaluation of their right-hand sides doesn't
	actually use any of the local names.
	Exercise

shows
	an example of a function that doesn't
	obey these restrictions, so that the alternative evaluator isn't
	equivalent to our scanning-out-names evaluator.

Sequential definition processing is more efficient and easier to
	implement than scanning out names.
	However, with sequential processing, the
	binding to which a name refers may depend on the order in which
	the statements in the body of a function are evaluated.
	In exercise

, we see that
	views may differ as to whether that is desirable.

The designers of Python support Alyssa on the
	following grounds: Eva is in principle correct—the assignments
